title: A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4)
summary: Defines the Border Gateway Protocol version 4 (BGP-4), the inter-autonomous-system routing protocol of the Internet, together with its companion RFC 1772. It was a draft standard and has been replaced by RFC 4271.

plainLanguage.summary: Networks use BGP to tell each other which roads they can reach, like big cities swapping maps.

questions: what are the bgp message types
how does bgp prevent routing loops
subtitle: How separate networks tell each other which destinations they can reach, in the first classless version of BGP.

tldr.problem: The Internet is made of many independently run Autonomous Systems, and each needs a way to learn which destinations the others can reach without exposing its internal routing.
tldr.mechanism: BGP-4 speakers open a TCP connection, send their full routing table once, then send incremental UPDATE messages that carry an IP prefix plus path attributes such as the list of ASs traversed.
tldr.outcome: This version is Draft Standard status and was obsoleted by RFC 4271, which is the current BGP-4 specification.

today: RFC 1771 has been obsoleted by RFC 4271, which is now the BGP-4 specification. It had itself replaced RFC 1654, and its status here is Draft Standard.

sections.title: What BGP-4 Does
sections.content:
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is an inter-Autonomous System routing protocol. Its main job is to exchange network reachability information with other BGP systems, including the list of Autonomous Systems (ASs) that the information has passed through. That list is enough to build a graph of AS connectivity, prune routing loops and enforce some policy decisions at the AS level.

BGP-4 adds mechanisms for classless interdomain routing: it advertises an IP prefix, drops the idea of network class, and allows routes, including AS paths, to be aggregated. BGP runs over a reliable transport. It uses TCP port 179, so it needs no update fragmentation, retransmission or sequencing of its own.

The policy model is hop by hop. A BGP speaker advertises to its peers in neighboring ASs only the routes that it uses itself. The RFC notes that BGP cannot support policies that need something like source routing.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP is how big networks tell each other what they can reach. Each one only passes along the roads it really uses itself.

sections.title: The Four BGP Messages
sections.content:
Every message starts with a fixed header: a 16-octet Marker, a 2-octet Length and a 1-octet Type. The smallest message is the 19-octet header alone and the largest is 4096 octets. Type codes are 1 OPEN, 2 UPDATE, 3 NOTIFICATION and 4 KEEPALIVE. The Marker is all ones for OPEN, or when no authentication information was sent. Otherwise it is computed by the chosen authentication mechanism, and it also lets a receiver detect loss of synchronization.

The first message each side sends is OPEN. It carries the version (4), the sender's AS number, a proposed Hold Time, a 4-octet BGP Identifier and optional parameters, such as authentication information. The Hold Time must be zero or at least three seconds, and each side uses the smaller of the two proposals.

An UPDATE advertises at most one feasible route and can also withdraw several routes. It holds a list of withdrawn prefixes, the path attributes, and the Network Layer Reachability Information (NLRI), which is a list of <length, prefix> pairs. A KEEPALIVE is just the 19-octet header. A NOTIFICATION reports an error with a code, a subcode and data, and the connection is then closed.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP has four kinds of notes: hello, news about roads, I am still here, and something went wrong. Every note starts with the same label saying how long it is and what kind it is.

sections.title: Path Attributes
sections.content:
Each route in an UPDATE comes with path attributes. They fall into four categories: well-known mandatory, well-known discretionary, optional transitive and optional non-transitive. Well-known attributes must be recognized by every implementation. A receiver that does not recognize an optional transitive attribute should accept the path and pass the attribute on with the Partial bit set. It quietly ignores an unrecognized non-transitive one.

The attributes defined here are ORIGIN (1), AS_PATH (2), NEXT_HOP (3), MULTI_EXIT_DISC (4), LOCAL_PREF (5), ATOMIC_AGGREGATE (6) and AGGREGATOR (7).

AS_PATH is the loop-prevention tool. When a route goes to a neighbor in another AS, the speaker prepends its own AS number. A route sent inside the same AS leaves the AS_PATH alone. Segments are either an unordered AS_SET or an ordered AS_SEQUENCE.
sections.plainLanguage: Each road announcement comes with sticky notes. One note lists every city it already passed through, so a city can see if the road would loop back to itself.

sections.title: The BGP State Machine
sections.content:
A connection with each peer moves through six states: Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm and Established. BGP starts in Idle, where it refuses incoming connections. A Start event initializes resources and starts the ConnectRetry timer, and the speaker tries to open the TCP connection while also listening for the peer.

Once the transport is up, each side sends OPEN and waits in OpenSent. If the peer's OPEN is acceptable, it sends a KEEPALIVE and moves to OpenConfirm. When a KEEPALIVE arrives, the session is Established and UPDATE messages can flow. Errors, Hold Timer expiry and unexpected events send a NOTIFICATION and drop back to Idle.

To avoid flapping on persistent errors, automatic restarts after an error should back off exponentially, starting at 60 seconds and doubling on each retry. If two speakers connect to each other at once, the connection initiated by the speaker with the higher BGP Identifier is kept.
sections.plainLanguage: Two neighbors greeting each other go step by step: knock, say hello, wait for hello back, then start chatting. If anything goes wrong they hang up and wait a bit before trying again.

sections.title: Handling Updates and Choosing Routes
sections.content:
When an UPDATE arrives, withdrawn prefixes are removed from the Adj-RIB-In, the table of routes learned from that peer. A new route replaces any older one with identical NLRI, and the speaker then runs its Decision Process. The routing tables are conceptually split into Adj-RIBs-In, the Loc-RIB of selected routes, and Adj-RIBs-Out for routes to advertise.

The Decision Process has three phases. Phase 1 computes a degree of preference for each route. Phase 2 picks the best route per destination and installs it in the Loc-RIB. Phase 3 disseminates the Loc-RIB to peers in neighboring ASs, and may aggregate routes. Local policy decides the degree of preference.

Ties in Phase 2 are broken first by lowest MULTI_EXIT_DISC when the local system is configured to consider it, then by the lowest interior cost to the NEXT_HOP. A remaining tie goes to the route from the speaker with the lowest BGP Identifier. When prefixes overlap, the more specific route takes precedence.
sections.plainLanguage: When news about roads comes in, a city checks it against its own rules, picks the best road for each place, and only then tells its neighbors about the road it picked.

sections.title: Errors and Security
sections.content:
A detected error produces a NOTIFICATION with an error code and subcode, after which the BGP connection is closed. The codes are 1 Message Header Error, 2 OPEN Message Error, 3 UPDATE Message Error, 4 Hold Timer Expired, 5 Finite State Machine Error and 6 Cease. Cease is used for an orderly close when no fatal error exists. The Data field carries the faulty value where that helps diagnosis.

If no KEEPALIVE or UPDATE arrives within the negotiated Hold Time, the peer is declared dead. KEEPALIVEs should come about every third of the Hold Time and never more often than once per second. If the negotiated Hold Time is zero, periodic KEEPALIVEs are not sent.

Security is left to optional authentication information in OPEN and to the transport. The RFC's Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: If a note is garbled or a neighbor goes quiet for too long, the city sends a short message explaining why and hangs up.
